Title: Measurement Invariance: definition and example in R | Towards Data Science
# Measurement Invariance: definition and example in R. How measurement invariance can improve your statistical inferences regarding human subjects. This property is referred to as measurement invariance or lack of bias. A common statistical method for establishing evidence of measurement invariance is through Multiple-Group Confirmatory Factor Analysis (MG-CFA). `Self_Esteem <- read.delim("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rafavsbastos/data/main/measurement%20invariance.dat")`. ## Coding measurement invariance. We will store results from our models in an empty matrix called *all.results*, where we will extract chi-square, degrees of freedom, RMSEA, CFI, and TLI. In our example, we are using self-esteem model, where we will fit a single-factor model with 10 observed variables. We will now write the code that specifies the model which we will use in the other analysis of measurement invariance. ### Baseline model. Now, we will do the baseline model (with no constraints across groups) using the measEq.syntax function from *semTools*. If you wish to see the results of this model, first you have to specify *as.character* to submit to lavaan. Now we will fit the baseline model in lavaan via *cfa* function. `fit.baseline <- cfa(model.baseline,. Of course, there is a lot of results under the printed one, but we will leave the overlook of the model as homework. `all.results[1,]<-round(data.matrix(fitmeasures(fit.baseline, fit.measures = c("chisq.scaled", "df.scaled","pvalue.scaled","rmsea.scaled","cfi.scaled","tli.scaled"))), digits=3)`. ### Thresholds Invariance Model. `#Fitting thresholds invariance model in lavaan via cfa function`. `fit.prop4 <- cfa(model.prop4,. `# Obtaining results from thresholds invariance model. `all.results[2,]<- round(data.matrix(fitmeasures(fit.prop4,fit.measures = c("chisq.scaled","df.scaled","pvalue.scaled","rmsea.scaled","cfi.scaled","tli.scaled"))),digits=3)`. ### The model with thresholds and loading invariance. `fit.prop7 <- cfa(model.prop7,. `all.results[3,] <- round(data.matrix(fitmeasures(fit.prop7, fit.measures = c("chisq.scaled", "df.scaled", "pvalue.scaled", "rmsea.scaled", "cfi.scaled", "tli.scaled"))), digits = 3)`. Using the measurement invariance for categorical data, we can see the models are getting better as models were constrained by imposing equality of thresholds and thresholds and loadings. paper, you can see that a lot needs to be done regarding guidelines to guarantee measurement invariance. As pointed out in the beginning, measurement invariance is a crucial part of inferences about group differences, and our measures need to take it into account before we run the following analysis. Rutkowski, Multiple-Group Invariance with Categorical Outcomes Using Updated Guidelines: An Illustration Using M plus and the lavaan/semTools Packages (2019), Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal.

results.title: A checklist for testing measurement invariance
results.content: By establishing whether factor loadings, intercepts and residual variances are equivalent in a factor model that measures a latent concept, we can assure that comparisons that are made on the latent variable are valid across groups or time. As long as there are at least two loadings and intercepts that are constrained equal across groups, we can make valid inferences about the differences between latent factor means in the model (Byrne, Shavelson & Muthén, 1989). Reporting the results After testing the invariance of the measurement model, the next step is to test the equality of factor means and correlations between the latent variables, across groups.

results.title: Short version of the smartphone addiction scale: Measurement invariance across gender | PLOS One
results.content: # Short version of the smartphone addiction scale: Measurement invariance across gender Roles Conceptualization, Investigation, Methodology, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing Affiliation School of Psychology, Inner Mongolia Normal University, Hohhot, China Affiliation Beidou College, Wuhan Qingchuan University, Wuhan, China Affiliation School of Psychology, Inner Mongolia Normal University, Hohhot, China Affiliation School of Psychology, Inner Mongolia Normal University, Hohhot, China Affiliation School of Psychology, Inner Mongolia Normal University, Hohhot, China Roles Conceptualization, Funding acquisition, Supervision, Writing – review & editing Affiliation College of Physical Education, Inner Mongolia Normal University, Hohhot, China # Short version of the smartphone addiction scale: Measurement invariance across gender ## Figures ## Abstract The Smartphone Addiction Scale Short Version (SAS-SV) has been widely used in research, but little is known about the measurement invariance across gender. SAS-SV was psychometrically robust in measuring the severity of smartphone addiction among college students, as well as the gender-based invariance. **Citation:** Yue H, Yue X, Liu B, Li X, Dong Y, Bao H (2023) Short version of the smartphone addiction scale: Measurement invariance across gender. The scalar invariance model (M3) was assessed by constraining factor loadings and item intercepts to be identical across the two gender groups and good fitting of the data to the model was shown (χ2/df = 2.288, RMSEA = 0.048, CFI = 0.985, SRMR = 0.033). Strict invariance of the scale (M4) was assessed by holding factor loadings, intercepts and residual item variance equal across male and female groups and good fitting of the data to the model was shown (χ2/df = 2.425, RMSEA = 0.051, CFI = 0.981, SRMR = 0.036). Moreover, raw score means of the two gender groups were compared, and the results indicated that males and females had an equivalent level of smartphone addiction. Identical SAS-SV scores from the two gender groups represented equal levels of smartphone addiction in male and female students. Therefore, the SAS-SV may be used with confidence to measure and compare the degree of smartphone addiction across gender in Chinese university student samples. Differences in SAS-SV scores between male and female college students indicated obvious gender differences in smartphone addiction, which were not due to measurement deviation of the scale items. Reliability and construct validity of the smartphone addiction scale short version (SAS-SV) in Iranian students.

results.title: Examining Appropriacy of CFI and TLI Cutoff Value in Multiple ...
results.content: Third, although previous studies have examined sev-eral fit indices across multiple conditions, they have not addressed the effect of several important factors (including the percentage of LOI items, the IRT model used, the values of the a and b parameter values, and the sample sizes used in the simulation) on the change in fit indices when determining an appropriate cutoff value. To address these three major limitations of previous studies, the present research employs a simulation to (a) evaluate the appropriateness of the proposed cutoff value of DCFI and DTLI .0.01 (Cheung & Rensvold, 2002) in an educational measurement context, and (b) examine the effects of several relevant factors on the change of fit indices for assessing MI using MG-CFA (the percentage of LOI items, the IRT model used, the values of the a and b parameter values, and the sample sizes used in the simulation). ## Present Study In this study, MG-CFA was used to investigate the per-formance of the CFI, TLI, and the RMSEA model fit indices in detecting scalar non-invariance in the presence of non-negligible MI induced by 0.5 difference in test characteristic curve (TCC) between the focal and the ref-erence groups on a simulated one-dimensional IRT-cali-brated test with 40 dichotomous items. In addition, the effect of five factors on change in the CFI, TLI, and the RMSEA model fit indices was investigated, including the percentage of DIF items (10% and 20%), IRT model used (2PL and 3PL), the a (0.5, 1.0, and 1.5) and the b (21 and 0, 1) parameter values, and the sample size (500, 1,000, and 2,000). Although the MH test procedure showed the presence of DIF items in the simulated test scores, the CFI, TLI, and the RMSEA fit indices seem to fail in capturing model fit deterioration due to the existence of measurement non-invariance at the scalar level. The results of the study showed that although the MH procedure detected the presence of DIF items, using the practical effect size criter-ion proposed by Cheung and Rensvold (2002) for the CFI and TLI fit indices failed to support the inference that the LOI was non-negligible (i.e., the simulated 0.5 difference between the focal and the reference groups).
